transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-07-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), John Li (AtlasPay), Sarah Nguyen (AtlasPay CTO), Mike O'Connor (AtlasPay Platform), Ava Chen (AtlasPay SRE)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping focused on benchmark planning and how AtlasPay's existing scripts integrate with Redwood's benchmark harness. Discussed streaming vs non-streaming test modes, target QPS, latency SLOs, and security/network constraints for dedicated runs.

Topics:
- Workload sizing: sequence length distribution, average generation tokens, peak concurrency
- Harness integration: python scripts, websocket streaming, load tools, auth and KMS
- Success criteria: p95/p99 latency, throughput (QPS), error rate <0.1%, cost per 1M tokens estimate
- Timeline: data + scripts by 7/22, quick turn-around config + test 7/28 week

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we know you have a busy week so plan is to run through the benchmark plan and the harness integration details. Carlos will cover the technical parts.
[00:18] Carlos: Hi all. quick agenda: what you can drop into our harness, streaming vs non streaming differences, what metrics we'll capture, and the recommended test matrix.
[00:27] John: Great. Our primary ask is to validate latency at scale for our payment confirmation flows. Typical gen length is about 40 tokens but we also have 5-10% long tails up to 300 tokens for dispute summaries.
[00:42] Sarah: And we need p95 under 450ms for the hosted path, ideally 300ms for dedicated. Cost also matters, so we'll want cost per generated 1k tokens ballpark.
[01:02] Carlos: ok good, important to separate streaming vs non-streaming. For streaming the client keeps a websocket open, tokens arrive incrementally — that changes the CPU/mem profile. Non-streaming is request->response, bigger single payloads. Our harness can run both modes.
[01:22] Mike: Our current scripts are python requests for REST, and a small node websocket client for streaming proofs. Are those ok to drop in?
[01:31] Maya: yes. if you can share both the rest script and the websocket example we'll wire them to our harness. we'll also give a reference locust/vegeta config.
[01:44] John: One thing: our client reuses a connection pool and uses prefix caching on our side for template prompts. Does Redwood support prefix/K V cache behavior?
[01:56] Carlos: Yes — sorry sometimes the transcription calls it K V cache or K V cache, but we mean KV cache support, and we have prefix caching options. For the benchmark we'll want to test cold-cache vs warm-cache. We recommend a matrix: cold start baseline, warm KV cache for steady-state, and burst scenarios.
[02:20] Sarah: For concurrency, typical steady-state is ~120 concurrent sessions, peak 600 for 2-3 minutes. QPS is around 25 steady, 110 peak.
[02:33] Carlos: That helps. We'll map that to concurrency and batch size in the harness. For token distribution please send us a histogram (e.g., percentiles for prompt+generation lengths).
[02:48] Mike: We have anonymized logs we can scrub and share. Also want to understand how streaming affects observed p95 — does p95 mean time to first token or time to final token?
[03:03] Maya: good question. We should define success metrics. For streaming we usually track time-to-first-byte (TTFB) and final completion latency. For AtlasPay I'd recommend TTFB p50/p95 and completion p95/p99.
[03:20] John: Completion p99 is what our SLAs are measured against internally.
[03:25] Carlos: noted. We'll configure the harness to capture both TTFB and final token completion. Also capture per-token throughput and server-side CPU/GPU utilization if we run on a dedicated pool.
[03:40] Sarah: What models will we test? We need to see a production-like variant — probably a 13B-class quantized model but we're open to Redwood recommendations.
[03:52] Carlos: We'll propose a couple: redwood-13b (quantized 4-bit) and a smaller 7B for cost/perf tradeoffs. Also include a 1-shot prompt and some longer few-shot templates. We'll note expected token multipliers.
[04:05] Mike: How do we run dedicated pool tests? We have a VPC restriction and require peering.
[04:13] Maya: For private/dedicated runs we can do a temporary dedicated pool in Redwood Dedicated with VPC peering. We'll need your VPC details and an allowed test window; that will require a short network pre-check.
[04:29] Ava: We'll provide the peering details. Security-wise, we require KMS integration and SOC2 evidence.
[04:36] Carlos: We'll share our SOC2 and KMS docs. For the benchmark we can obfuscate payloads, but the live dedicated run will be behind your peering.
[04:47] John: On harness instrumentation — does Redwood's har ness support measuring client-side retry behavior? Our SDK does exponential backoff.
[04:55] Carlos: The harness can replay your client behavior or emulate retries. If you give us your SDK's retry parameters we can model that. For the initial runs we'll do straight-line no-retry to baseline.
[05:07] Sarah: We also want to capture cost projections. Can the harness output estimated token costs and GPU-hours?
[05:13] Maya: Yes, the harness will report tokens, tokens per request, and we can append estimated cost using Redwood pricing buckets or your Dedicated rate card. We'll include an approx cost per 1M tokens for each model.
[05:26] John: Great. For benchmarking cadence, thinking: initial functional/compatibility run (streaming + non-streaming) -> throughput runs (1-2 hours) -> stress runs (4 hours overnight).
[05:39] Carlos: Sounds good. We'll do a smoke test first to ensure scripts run in harness. Then a 2-hour throughput run with warm cache, then a stress test. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and error rates.
[05:51] Mike: Any recommended load tools? We used locust in the past; also have a proprietary runner.
[05:58] Carlos: Locust is fine; we have reference locust scenarios and a lightweight python harness that wraps our API with concurrency control. We'll send those.
[06:09] John: One more: streaming mode for us is critical because UI shows partial confirmations as tokens arrive. So TTFB is a hard requirement.
[06:17] Maya: Understood. We'll highlight the streaming TTFB numbers separately in the report.
[06:25] Sarah: Timeline recap?
[06:27] Maya: You (AtlasPay) provide scripts and token distribution by 7/22. We'll return a recommended config by 7/22 and the harness repo by 7/20. Schedule the dedicated 2-hour run in the week of 7/28.
[06:38] Carlos: On data side, please sanitize logs. For long-tail examples we may sample a small set to debug generation quality.
[06:46] John: We'll do that. Also curious about fallbacks — if dedicated capacity is full, can we automatically fallback to hosted variants?
[06:55] Carlos: Yes, Redwood supports routing policies and fallback to compatible model variants or hosted capacity. We'll include those options in the config. Bear in mind token cost and latency will change on fallback.
[07:07] Mike: Any recommended batching settings? We saw in prior tests that larger batch sizes hurt p99 but help throughput.
[07:15] Carlos: Right — that's the classic tradeoff. For your latency targets we recommend conservative batch sizes for p99 sensitive flows, and larger batches for background or async flows. We'll provide suggested batch size curves.
[07:29] Sarah: What about measuring cold-starts?
[07:33] Carlos: We'll schedule cold-start runs by restarting the model workers between small runs or using an empty cache window. We'll record time-to-warm and impact on p95/p99.
[07:44] John: Okay. Anything else?
[07:46] Maya: We'll also include an evaluation checklist: what success looks like — p95/p99 targets, error rate, cost per 1M tokens, and a pass/fail on streaming TTFB.
[07:58] Sarah: Sounds good. Please include security docs.
[08:01] Maya: will do.

(there's some cross talk and background noise)
[08:25] Carlos: quick note — when you share scripts, include env vars we need for auth, but don't include secrets. We'll use a test key.
[08:33] John: acknowledged.
[09:05] Maya: recap of next steps...
[09:10] Maya: we will send harness repo by 7/20; you'll send scripts and token hist by 7/22; we'll prepare config and suggested models by 7/22; schedule dedicated run for week of 7/28. We'll also exchange SOC2/KMS docs by 7/21.
[09:28] Sarah: ok thanks, let's follow up in the tracker.
[09:32] Maya: thanks everyone. will put items into the CRM and follow up.

Meeting end.
